history.summary: Baseline, taken at the state following the UI-registry work: Deck defaults to count-only so draw piles report their size again, AutoUI and Die3D moved off the boardsmith/ui barrel, and the board-side ValidElement became BoardTarget. Also introduces the contract itself — ENGINE_CONTRACT and ENGINE_REVISION are exported from the boardsmith root so the platform can read the vendored engine's revision at runtime.

Contract fingerprints widened after an adversarial review found them narrower than claimed: surfaceHash now includes prototype members (games call methods, and renaming one used to move neither hash), and the payload fixture now boots through GameRunner with a simultaneous opening step so flow state, isMyTurn and availableActions are covered — the blank-action-bar layer, previously invisible.

Checkpoint retention: games can bound per-action undo checkpoints with checkpoints:{max|enabled}; snapshot.actionCheckpoints is now a {baseIndex,entries} window, and a pruned undo target is refused with a message naming the policy

Player-facing state changes: the default player palette now has 16 colors instead of 8 (the first 8 are unchanged, so existing games keep their colors) so a game can seat up to the platform's 16-player maximum without shipping its own palette; separately, a typed array (Uint8Array etc.) in game state now serializes as a compact {__typedArray,data} base64 shape and restores as its real type instead of silently inflating ~7x into a plain object, and an ArrayBuffer or DataView in state is now refused at serialization time rather than silently becoming {}.

Player gains a first-class status field ('active' | 'dormant' | 'eliminated', default 'active') plus an isActive getter — it serializes into the tree and is visible in every seat's player view, so hosts can read seat liveness directly, and TurnOrder.ACTIVE_ONLY now filters on it instead of an undeclared 'eliminated' property. Also: every enterText selection is now length-bounded (DEFAULT_TEXT_MAX_LENGTH = 256 when a game sets no maxLength), and CheckpointPolicy is exported from the boardsmith root and boardsmith/session so a published bundle can name the type for GameDefinition.checkpoints.
Action builder gains .validate(fn): a submit-time, whole-submission gate returning true | false | a message string, enforced on both the one-shot and incremental execute paths.
Engine exports turnSequence() and orderSeatsByTurn(): recover the running order eachPlayer already resolved, and arrange seats for display without dropping or duplicating any.

Renamed ActionBuilder.suppressFromDock() to .suppressFromActionPanel() and its actionMetadata field to match: 'Action Panel' is now the single name for the control surface (the 'dock' synonym is retired everywhere, including the --dock-h CSS custom property, now --action-panel-h).

Added Game.messageTo(audience, text, data): a per-seat game-log channel for hidden-information games, withheld server-side in toJSONForPlayer and createPlayerView so an unaddressed seat never receives the message. game.messages gains an optional 'to' audience field (absent = public). Also removed GameShell's showHistory prop: a game can no longer suppress the log.

Game.toJSON() no longer duplicates phase/messages/settings into the generic attributes bag; they are top-level fields only. Fixes a messageTo leak where attributes.messages shipped every seat's private log unredacted.

The message log moved out of the serialized game tree into GameStateSnapshot.messageLog, stored once per snapshot with an ActionCheckpoint.messageCount watermark for undo. Persisted state is now flat in checkpoints.max instead of multiplying the log by it.

Actions gain .disabled(ctx) => string|false; Game.getTutorialDisabledActions renamed to getDisabledActions and now merges action-level disabled reasons with tutorial gate reasons; disabledActions is projected outside tutorials.

execute() flow nodes are undo-transparent by default; only execute(fn, { irreversible: true }) fences undo/rewind (Game.getExecuteNodeCompletions renamed to getIrreversibleCommitCount). PlayerGameState also gains restoreEpoch, a per-seat counter of checkpoint restores clients use to invalidate element ids held from the replaced runner.

Epic #24 engine changes, landed together: (1) a flow that completes inside startFlow() now publishes its winners, so a game that ends during setup reports a result instead of none; (2) checkpoints:{enabled:false} sheds an inherited checkpoint window rather than silently keeping it; (3) randomness policy moved to GameOptions.randomness, applied inside Game's own constructor, so 'forbidden' forbids draws from the game's FIRST instruction (subclass constructors included) and is stripped from _constructorOptions so no host policy persists into a snapshot — RandomnessPolicy is exported from boardsmith/runtime, forbidRandomness() is private, an undo random fence closes RNG scumming, and GameRunner.checkpointWindow() is public so the fence reports the real cause of a missing checkpoint; (4) an action's ActionResult.data now reaches its caller across engine/runtime/session/cli and the board on every transport, via useActionController.lastActionResult (BUG-017).

Phase 68 async/simultaneous play support. FOUR surface changes a consumer must react to: (1) SnapshotSessionAdapters.broadcast meta gains a REQUIRED turnBoundary { key, dueSeats } — an un-updated adapter is a COMPILE ERROR, deliberately, because the host is what must publish the round identity to each seat. (2) The action and selectionStep ops gain a REQUIRED boundaryKey naming the round a submission was composed against; ONE comparison site refuses a submission that names a closed round, with "The round you acted in has closed; reload to see the current round." REQUIRED is a TYPE requirement only: at runtime the guard keys on the PRESENCE of the field, so an op that omits boundaryKey is passed through UNGUARDED. The guard is therefore INERT until the host stamps the key, and the host is where it must be stamped — echo back the key you sent on game_state. New exports flowBoundaryKey (boardsmith) and STALE_SUBMISSION_MESSAGE / SUBMISSION_OP_TYPES (boardsmith/session) are the pieces a host needs. (3) A new convertSeatToBot host lifecycle op converts a seat mid-game, acknowledges it as OpResult.convertedSeat and drives the existing bot pump; it is idempotent on re-wake and REFUSES a finished game rather than silently no-opping. It carries no difficulty level, on purpose: a host-held seat-to-bot level map is a privilege-escalation surface. (4) position.frameData is now serialized and relinked by the SAME general flow-variable serializer as position.variables; the previousPlayer / previousPlayerSeat special case is gone, so a live element in frame data survives a broadcast instead of throwing DataCloneError — and previousPlayerSeat no longer appears in the payload. That is what moved payloadHash. COMPATIBILITY, measured rather than assumed: revision, NOT bundleProtocol. Diffing the runtime export names of all three platform entrypoints against r14 shows ADDITIONS ONLY — nothing removed, nothing renamed. A published rules.js never composes an op (the executor builds ops from the wire body), so every already-built bundle keeps running. The two REQUIRED fields are a wire change for whatever COMPOSES an op or a broadcast — the games worker, and a published bundle own GameShell UI — not for the rules; and because an absent boundaryKey is unguarded, an un-updated host also keeps working and merely forfeits the protection until it stamps the key.

The automaton is a BOT, not an AI, across the whole engine surface (ShufflewickPub #28). adapters.aiSeats -> botSeats; the aiTurn/aiSuggest ops -> botTurn/botSuggest; playerOptions.aiLevel -> botLevel; the gameDefinition/manifest 'ai' block -> 'bot'; the boardsmith/ai and boardsmith/ai-trainer subpaths -> boardsmith/bot and boardsmith/bot-trainer; the --ai and --ai-level dev flags -> --bot and --bot-level; SlotStatus 'ai' -> 'bot'; AIController -> BotController. Three types that were all spelled AIConfig were disambiguated first: the game's strategy hooks are BotStrategy, which seats are bots is BotSeatConfig, and the alias that existed only to tell them apart is gone. RENAMES, so this is a BREAKING surface change: every consumer and every published bundle must be rebuilt against it.

World mode, step one (ShufflewickPub #35 item 2): Game gains enableWorldMode/worldMode, definePartition, adoptSubtree, evictSubtree, touchedPartitions and clearTouchedPartitions, so a resident engine can hold only the partitions a command names and pay O(room) per action instead of O(world). ADDITIONS ONLY -- nothing removed or renamed, and snapshot mode (every published board game) is behaviourally unchanged. World mode changes exactly one thing when it is switched on: an element reference in an attribute serializes as { __elementId } instead of the positional { __elementRef: branch }, because a non-resident partition shifts every later sibling index and a branch path recorded against the full world resolves against a partial one to a DIFFERENT element. In world mode an __elementId that cannot resolve is kept verbatim rather than becoming undefined, so a reference into a non-resident partition survives the next checkpoint. moveToInternal -- the one shared re-parent path -- now marks BOTH endpoints' partitions after its existing throws, so a rejected move marks nothing and a cross-partition move still reports the destination the command never read.

r18: fail-loud authoring errors — ReservedAttributeError, ConditionEvaluationError and PlayerFacingError are exported; a crashing condition, an unknown flow action and detected tree corruption now throw; a failed execute() rolls back and its raw message no longer reaches players.

r18: fail-loud authoring errors — ReservedAttributeError, ConditionEvaluationError and PlayerFacingError are exported; a crashing condition, an unknown flow action and detected tree corruption now throw; a failed execute() rolls back and its raw message no longer reaches players (a PlayerFacingError's does).

r19: isEngineRootField / engineRootFieldAudience / GAME_ROOT_FIELD_AUDIENCE are exported so a game can defer to the engine's root-field audiences; enumerateLegalMoves throws on a bad seat instead of returning []; MCTSBot.play resolves to null (with lastStallReason) when a seat's own information state offers no searchable move, instead of throwing and locking the table.

r20: message() and messageTo() take a game-supplied per-line type that survives to the client, so a log can classify its own entries; animateTo() gives animation events the same server-enforced audience messageTo() has.

r21: game.refreshAwaitingActions() lets a simultaneous step's awaiting set grow for a seat that becomes eligible mid-step; game.pruneMessages() caps the log safely now that each MessageEntry carries a seq identity and ActionCheckpoint records messageSeq instead of a prefix length.

r21: game.refreshAwaitingActions() lets a simultaneous step's awaiting set grow for a seat that becomes eligible mid-step; game.pruneMessages() caps the log safely — ActionCheckpoint.messageCount is now the log's ABSOLUTE length and the game tracks how many entries were evicted, so pruning no longer corrupts earlier checkpoints.

r23: NotSimulableError lets a game say a move is legal but unresolvable from a bot's redacted information state, so MCTS drops it from the search instead of logging a stack per rollout; enumerateLegalMoves re-checks condition and validate rather than trusting the flow state's frozen availableActions.

r25: boardsmith/persistence is a new platform entrypoint carrying the persistence validation core -- the reserved persist/persistPrivate channel names, PERSIST_MAX_COMMIT_BYTES, readPersistCommit, toStartPayload, drainResolutionInputs, the session-kind vocabulary and a pure cross-session store. ShufflewickPub's games worker now re-exports it from games/src/persistence.ts instead of restating it, so boardsmith dev's MultiplayerHost runs the SAME validators the platform's Durable Object does (ShufflewickPub #41).

Tracker sweep, two surface changes recorded together (they were originally r25 and r26 on the pre-rebase branch, renumbered because that branch forked before boardsmith/persistence existed): (1) a withheld attribute now restores as unknown and throws on read (RedactedAttributeError, GameElement.isAttributeRedacted / redactedAttributes) instead of silently holding its class-field default; (2) actionStep gains turnScope, and FlowPosition/FlowState gain turnRun/turnScopeUndeclared, so undo reach can span the frame boundary a loop iteration or a sibling action step creates.

World mode is declared at construction: GameOptions.worldMode replaces Game#enableWorldMode(), so a world is what a game IS rather than something switched on afterwards, and a world's seats are no longer capped by the size of the player palette.

The session-kind vocabulary is match | world, and a refusal that names no error is a refusal (ShufflewickPub #47 and #90). BREAKING, by deletion: the two round-era kinds are gone, and so is everything that existed only for them -- seatsHumans; the store's order routing, roster and enrol; ResolutionInputs / drainResolutionInputs / RESOLUTION_SEAT and the two reserved resolve-action argument keys; MultiplayerHost.resolveRound; and the --kind / --resolve-action dev flags, which after the deletion selected no behaviour at all. store.commit and store.readForSession no longer take a kind, because neither reads one any more. The sealed-key rule for world is allow:'seated', the same as a match: the resolver's write-any-player's-key bypass was a consequence of SEATLESSNESS, not of authority, and a resident world is seated at every write, so there is nothing for a bypass to rescue. Separately, acceptExecuteResult now REFUSES a { success: false } carrying no error (an empty string counts as none) instead of inverting it into a success -- a game that refused a move without saying why used to have the refusal silently become an accepted move.

The dev host's persistPrivate strip now refuses a divergent per-player secret with the same actionable error production's executor throws (previously it silently committed the first defined value), and in world mode Game#touchedPartitions now reports attribute-level changes to resident partitions -- detected by comparing each partition's serialized form against a baseline captured at definePartition/adoptSubtree/clearTouchedPartitions -- so a write reached through an element.game or element.parent walk into an undeclared partition is checkpointed instead of silently reverting on eviction; clearTouchedPartitions re-baselines, and evictSubtree preserves a not-yet-checkpointed content change as a kept touch-mark.

The world wire's world_state message now carries presence: number[] | null -- the platform-composed live present-seat set, per seat, derived and never stored, empty after a park, null when the host page has no live claim (left vs reconnecting not distinguished) -- and WorldShell/useWorldHost hand it to a bundle's world UI as the presence prop and useWorld().presence. Host pages must include the field when composing world_state; the whole wire is now part of payloadHash.

Element-level visibility lives on GameElement rather than only on Piece (issue #162): setVisibility, showToAll, showToOwner, hideFromAll, addVisibleTo, showOnlyTo, hideFrom and clearVisibility moved up from Piece, which keeps every one of them by inheritance. Purely additive -- no behaviour changes for any existing game -- and a Space now has both halves: hideFromAll/showOnlyTo govern THE SPACE ITSELF, contentsHidden/addZoneVisibleTo govern its CONTENTS. A game modelling occupancy as a room's own visibility no longer has to hand-write a VisibilityState literal against setVisibilityInternal.

World mode's dirty-set pass is one serialization per resident partition per command, not three, and no longer searches the tree for each root (ShufflewickPub #316). Game#touchedPartitions (an idempotent getter that serialized every resident partition) and Game#clearTouchedPartitions (which serialized them again to re-baseline) are REPLACED by a single consuming Game#takeTouchedPartitions(), which reports what changed and re-baselines from the fingerprints it just computed. Game#partitionBaseline(id) hands back the pre-command bytes and parent id the platform used to obtain by serializing the whole resident set a third time for its rollback copy, and Game#partitionRoot(id) returns a declared root without the depth-first getElementById walk that made every O(resident) pass O(resident squared). Behaviour of the dirty set is unchanged -- moves and attribute changes are reported exactly as before -- and snapshot mode is untouched.

The world-mode dirty-set comparison is scoped to the partitions a command REACHED, so per-command CPU is the room and not the resident world (ShufflewickPub #295). The engine marks every door it owns -- Game#getElementById and an element's all/first/firstN/last/lastN/atId/atBranch/parent/children -- the new Game#reachPartition lets the platform mark the one door it owns (the root a command's partition(name) answers with), and the new Game#readingOnly turns marking off for a read the platform guarantees cannot write, which is what a declaration and a view are. A partition nothing handed out keeps its baseline and is not serialized. Measured at 256 resident partitions of ~10 KB: 12.8 ms per command down to 0.28 ms.

The world wire gains a world_events message and WorldShell hands its payloads to a game's UI (ShufflewickPub #331). A world's narration is its routed events, and until now they reached no screen: the platform routed them per audience and put them on the socket, and the host page answered the frame with a view request and dropped the payloads, so anything a world narrated that left no residue in its tree -- an emote, combat text, a line somebody said -- was undeliverable and a game had to write it into its own stored state to show it. The host now sends { source: 'shufflewick-world', type: 'world_events', events: [{ scope, payload }] }, a SECOND message rather than a field on world_state, because state is re-pushed whenever any part of it moves and a line carried on it would be redelivered on every later push. useWorldHost appends each delivery into a new events ref, bounded at the new exported WORLD_NARRATION_KEPT (200, oldest dropped) and deliberately NOT counted as heardFromHost, since narration carries no view, seat or commands; WorldShell passes it as an events prop and through useWorld().events, and WorldNarration is exported from boardsmith/ui for a UI to declare the prop with. Purely additive to every existing message: a host that never sends world_events leaves the log empty, and a UI that ignores the prop is unchanged. Host pages must send the new message for a world's narration to be deliverable at all; the whole wire is part of payloadHash, which is what moved.

boardsmith/world ships the world runner core: residency, rollback baselines, dirty-set accumulation, per-seat view, event routing, schedule semantics, the partition-store interface, the refusals and the declaration types. The platform runs this instead of its own copy, and a launched world pins the revision that carries it.

A world's verbs are Actions. worldAction() and worldClockAction() replace the flat command table; the seat's offer is its enumerated actions as ActionMetadata; ActionDefinition gains an optional world block carrying needs and seatless; ScheduleRequest names an action rather than a command and takes scalar args only. The world command contract types are deleted.

A world action can take back a keyed timer with ctx.world.cancel(key), and boardsmith/world exports resumeDueOf() -- the inverse of catchUpPlan's fold, which a host stamps a failed occurrence's retry with so the fold is not lost.

One backend interface with a declared capability set. boardsmith.json declares backend: table or world; the manifest carries a resolved capabilities object whose members (table, world, undo, spectators, bots, asyncPlay, joinInProgress, crossSessionState) replace the per-flag fields. GameDefinition.minPlayers and maxPlayers are optional and a world-only bundle carries no playerCount.

One shell for tables and worlds: PlayShell owns the shared chrome (sidebar, board region, action bar) and WorldShell mounts the action controller over it, so a world is drawn by the bundle's shell rather than by a generic surface. WorldNarration carries text and type, world_state carries players, and a world resolves its own pick choices locally. The world.ui manifest field is gone: boardsmith build always emits the world entry, and a world backend that built no world surface is refused.

ABI break, recorded late: r38 made world.maxPlayers required inside the world block, so readWorldDefinition refuses every world bundle built before it. That invalidates published world bundles, which is exactly what bundleProtocol exists to signal, and r38 left the number alone. Bundle protocol 1 becomes 2 here. Every world bundle must be rebuilt and republished.

The payload fixture now projects a world view: one seat's {player, state, phase} from a five-seat village whose declaration names a subset of its partitions with one resident partition it does not name, so a world view's two prunes, the partitions a seat declared and the game root's roster, are fingerprinted rather than invisible. Carries #181 and #186 themselves: a seat's view no longer ships the whole roster, and emit(scope, payload, narration?) gives a world a log line the shared shell renders.

A world's OFFER is fingerprinted alongside its view. offersFor has decided which verbs every seat is given since #169 and no fixture reached it, so #187's fix (a disabled action whose every candidate is greyed is offered with its reason, while an enabled one with no answerable question is still dropped) changed what every seat in every world sees and moved neither hash. The payload fixture now projects one seat's offer over four verbs covering every decision the enumerator makes, and a coverage table plus test makes any platform-facing world verb the fixture does not drive fail the suite instead of being described in a comment.
worlds: player commands carry a durable order identity and hosts answer a repeat from its receipt (#195); world.stateVersion is declared in the rules and derived into the manifest (#194)
worlds: a bundle may declare world.migration, moving a live world one stateVersion forward (partitions and queued event arguments, all-or-nothing); WorldEngine gains migratePartition (#200)

worlds and tables agree on choice identity: the engine's choice matcher moved to src/engine/action/choice-matching.ts, which the browser action controller now imports instead of reimplementing, and it resolves a string id shorthand and an identifying-subset object everywhere the engine already did (#219)

worlds can grow: world.migration.create adds durable partition roots in the same durable step as an upgrade, world.createPartition builds a root the first time a declaration names it, and a world's own elements are minted above a reserved id floor so world.maxPlayers can change on a live world (#218)

a world written before the construction-id floor is lifted onto it once, at its next start: one offset across every partition and every queued event, so a pre-floor world's seat count can change without its stored roots colliding with the wider construction (#223)

A step's needs() context now carries world -- the indexed, read-only WorldResidency that execute and a bundle's view(seat, world) already receive -- so a later round reaches a root an earlier round declared by name instead of searching the resident tree for it; readOnlyProjection also stopped wrapping its own output, which restores the identity a projected element had lost and takes a 500-root finder from 80x the live tree to 17x. The offer fixture now hashes the declaration WALK and not only its answer, which is why this revision exists at all: the walk was claimed as covered from r-#187 onward and was not (ShufflewickPub#374)

WorldAction gains chooseElements -- the plural of chooseElement, which two of the world's own refusals already told authors to reach for and which was not on the facade -- and chooseFrom now forwards multiSelect, so a world action can ask for a GROUP rather than one of a thing. A world's multiSelect always resolves to an array (the engine's form may return undefined to mean single; this one may not), so the argument type is knowable from the call. dependsOn stays refused: it is a cross-product in a single-shot protocol, and a dynamic BOUND does not need it (ShufflewickPub#376)

A declaration is stamped: commandPartitions and offerPartitions now take the instant the dispatch is happening at -- a command's stamped arrival, a scheduled event's due, an offer's own now -- and a needs() context reaches it as world.now, the same instant execute is about to be given. Without it a world whose partitions are TIMED could not tell a due one from a future one and had to declare every active one, which is O(world) in the mode whose argument is that a command costs O(room). No presence, deliberately: residency that depended on who is connected would differ between two watchers of one world. The runner's declare and declareOffers take the stamp through, so the parent must send it (ShufflewickPub#375)

A world's element-id allocation is durable state a host persists and hands back (ShufflewickPub #377). Game#worldIdAllocation()/#adoptWorldIdAllocation() expose the counter; WorldEngine#nextElementId() reports it; runner.genesis(), runner.createPartition() and runner.migrateCreate() now answer { ...bytes, nextElementId } so a host cannot write a minted root without the stamp that produced it; createWorld() takes it back as options.nextElementId. A cold world built without one REFUSES to create a partition on demand (new platform refusal allocation-undeclared) instead of minting an id a stored, unloaded root already owns, and adoptSubtree() refuses bytes that prove a declared stamp is stale. worldIdAllocationOf() derives the stamp once from stored bytes as the supported repair. Read-only world.partition(name) now reads the indexed root table instead of walking the resident tree (ShufflewickPub #381).

A world's panel can re-ask ONE pick with the arguments bound so far (ShufflewickPub #378). New WorldEngine verbs pickPartitions() and resolvePick(), and runner.declarePick()/resolvePick() beside them: a world's offer is enumerated in one frame with nothing bound, so a selection whose multiSelect bounds or choices callback read an earlier selection's value resolved to the unbounded fallback and reached the browser as a cap it could not use. An unbounded multiSelect now OMITS max on a world offer instead of serializing Infinity, which JSON writes as null and the action panel read as a cap of zero. The world wire gains the world_pick request and world_pick_result answer; a host that does not implement them leaves a world's later picks answered from the one-shot offer, as before.

A world's OFFER cannot write to the world it is describing (ShufflewickPub #384). Everything the offer path runs -- an action's condition, its disabled rule, a choices/elements callback, a prompt, a display, a multiSelect -- now receives the same read-only projection (world-readonly.ts, #219) that a declaration and world.view already receive, for both ctx.game and ctx.world.partition, and runs with reach-marking suspended (Game#readingOnly) the way viewFor does. Game#getActionDisabledReason and ActionExecutor#getChoices take an optional trailing 'reading' game so the rule stays ONE function evaluated one way: enforcement passes nothing and still sees the live game. An offer-time write was previously accepted, appeared in every watcher's next frame, was never checkpointed, and was reverted at the next hibernation with nobody told.

A migration is one atomic step that can read across roots (ShufflewickPub #379). The runner's migratePartition() and migrateCreate() are REPLACED by a single migrateAll(stored, ctx): every stored root is adopted before any hook runs, the per-root partition hook normalizes each one, create() adds this version's new roots, the new world.migration.finalize(game, { partition, names, from, to }) hook reads and writes across every root -- transformed and newly created alike -- and only then is anything serialized. So an existing root whose new value is derived from another existing root is expressible, and the answer does not depend on the order a host listed its keys in. WorldEngine gains migrateFinalize(). Everything still lands in the host's one transaction; a hook that throws leaves every original byte and the stored version untouched.

A world may declare that its player commands are CHRONOLOGICAL (ShufflewickPub #380). New WorldDefinition.ordering: 'arrival' (the default, and what every world did before this) or 'chronological', which gates each player command behind every event already due at that player's arrival instant, run in nominal order. It is for a chain that cannot be predeclared -- an event that creates a contract and schedules the next decision cannot name that decision's partitions until the earlier one commits. Bounded and yielding: one drainBatch at a time, at most the new catchUpRounds budget (default 8), with a turn for the runtime between each; running out, or meeting an event that refuses, applies the command over a world still behind rather than refusing it. The player's arrival instant, order identity and receipt are untouched, and a replayed order is answered from its receipt without running the clock. An unrecognised world.ordering is refused as bundle-not-a-world at construction.

A world's host now stamps every dispatch with the acting seat's DURABLE activity watermark (ShufflewickPub #383). ctx.world.activity carries {seat, at, since, inactiveSince}: at is the arrival instant of this seat's last ACCEPTED command, as of BEFORE the command carrying it, and inactiveSince is at ?? since -- the one number a gameplay inactivity deadline is written against. since is when the world began recording, so an occupied world upgraded into this feature reports its seats as idle since the upgrade rather than since 1970. A seat-owned scheduled event is handed its OWNER's watermark, which is what lets an irreversible cleanup deadline recheck whether the player came back; the world's own events carry null. Refusals, drained events, presence hooks and migrations never move a watermark, and it never moves backwards. WorldCommandStamp, WorldEventStamp and WorldOfferStamp all carry activity and a host must supply it; the local store keeps it per seat and fixes its recording epoch on first open.

A world may ask the platform to convert PLATFORM CREDITS into the game's own currency, and is told it cannot yet (ShufflewickPub #382). ctx.world.convertCredits({credits}) is declared and refuses every time with the new caller-owned code credit-conversion-unavailable, whose message states plainly that nothing was charged and nothing was granted and that the command has been unwound. It is shipped as a declared hole on purpose: ShufflewickPub has no currency system yet and the rate, bounds, quantum and reversal policy are undecided, and a game with no boundary to call writes its own payments -- running checkout, holding card details, trusting a browser about a debit and granting a paid reward twice. The signature commits to nothing but whole-number credits and one-way conversion; there is deliberately no method converting game currency back. Separately, the surface fingerprint now covers the WORLD_REFUSALS registry's codes and owners, which it never did: the park ladder branches on them (platform parks after two, game dead-letters, caller does neither), so adding a code or moving one between owners changes what the platform does to a live world and must mint a revision.

A checkpoint carries the allocation stamp its command minted under (#224). runner.serialize() answers { partitions, nextElementId } and WorldPartitionWriter.writeCheckpoint takes that whole checkpoint, so a host cannot store a grown partition without its stamp. #377 made the stamp durable and named three roads that move it -- genesis, on-demand creation, migration -- and left out the one every game takes: room.create() inside an action advances the same counter, so the next fresh runner was built below its own store and adoptSubtree refused the bytes that host had itself just written. A stale stamp is now the coded, platform-owned refusal allocation-stale instead of a bare Error charged to the game, so a park ladder can act on it; boardsmith dev repairs such a world off that refusal with worldIdAllocationOf. New WORLD_DURABILITY_FIXTURE puts the four shapes a host must persist into payloadHash, because they are types and surfaceHash cannot see them.

A new caller-owned refusal, world-catching-up (ShufflewickPub #395). A world declaring ordering: chronological asked not to be overtaken, and the platform implemented that as a four-times-larger drain budget -- which is an ordering guarantee only while the world is less than one budget behind. Past that the command was applied over a world still behind, silently, which is exactly the overtaken state the declaration exists to prevent, and no signal reached the handler, the client or the log. The command is now refused instead, and the refusal is CALLER-owned like rate-limited and for the same reason: well-formed traffic, world untouched, and a park ladder must never read a world that is merely behind as a world in trouble. Sending it again is safe -- an order's durable identity (#368) makes the repeat run exactly once -- and the platform re-arms before answering, so the catch-up is already continuing.

A migration may be run a page at a time when it need not see every root (ShufflewickPub #402). runner.migrationNeedsEveryRoot() answers whether the bundle declares finalize -- the hook #379 added so a migration can derive one root's value from another in either direction -- and the presence of it is the whole declaration of whether paging is safe, so no new authoring surface exists. migrateAll's context gains allNames (every root the WORLD holds, since create must know which names are taken and a refusal is about the world rather than the page) and runCreate (which single page adds this version's new roots). A page transforms and answers only the roots it was handed; paging a migration that declares finalize is refused by name rather than run against a half-migrated world. WORLD_DURABILITY_FIXTURE gains both context shapes, because they are types and surfaceHash cannot see one.

The engine declares formatHash: the serialization format of a world's durable partitions, measured as a round trip over a committed corpus of partition bytes. It is what lets the platform move a live world onto a newer runner instead of pinning it to its launch engine for life.

A migration re-baselines the roots it serialized, so a migrated partition may be evicted (ShufflewickPub #407). A migration is the one write path that does not run through a dispatch, so nothing consumed the engine's touch-marks afterwards: the engine went on believing every transformed root differed from storage, Game#evictSubtree keeps the mark of a change it believes was never checkpointed, and the world's next command found a touched root id it could no longer name and refused with partition-not-resident -- for good. So evicting a migrated partition, which is the entire saving paged migration exists for (#402), produced a correct migration and an unplayable world. WorldEngine gains migrateBaseline(names) and Game gains rebaselinePartitions(ids): the current bytes of exactly these roots are what the host now holds, so the baseline moves and any mark on them is dropped. runner.migrateAll calls it over exactly the names it just serialized, after it has taken them, since those bytes and the host's transaction are one thing. Nothing a host must call: platforms should now delete the comment in their paged migrate op and evict each page.

A world's roster can now SHRINK. Two changes, both for ShufflewickPub #399. (1) `WorldEngine.unseat(player)` retires a seat's holder, so a departed player's chair can be given to somebody else; before this the roster was add-only and the only way to reclaim a chair was to throw the isolate away and rebuild it, which on a host that caps a world's lifetime isolates means ordinary churn kills the world. It forgets a mapping and moves nothing in the world. (2) A bundle may declare `world.vacate`, the name of one of its own seated verbs, which a host runs for a seat that is leaving so the game can give that player's ground back; `createWorld` answers it beside `seatCount`, and `readWorldDefinition` refuses a name that answers to no verb, a seatless one, or one that asks a question. Returning the ground before reissuing the chair is the HOST's ordering to keep -- the engine cannot check it. A bundle that declares nothing behaves exactly as it did and its chairs stay held for life. formatHash is unchanged, so a live world may cross this revision.

A world engine gains viewsFor(players): a whole audience projected in one call. A fan-out is the shape a world spends its time in, and asking seat by seat serialized the resident tree in full once per watcher -- only the redaction on top of it is ever about the seat. Measured on a 500-seat plaza of 200 public stalls (37 KB a view), describing the world to everybody cost 213 ms, and 148 ms of that was the shared pass run again for each of them; the batch spends it once, for a 3.3x cut in the projection half of a notice. No view changes: the declaration, the residency it pulls in, the redaction and both prunes stay per seat, and the conformance suite holds the batch's answers against viewFor's. The runner's viewsFor now asks the engine once instead of looping; the platform's child op is unchanged. Stored partition bytes are untouched, so formatHash does not move and a live world crosses onto this revision with no gate.

A world's view no longer says who is looking, so ONE answer can be sent to a whole audience. WIRE CHANGE: the envelope is {state, phase} -- the seat number is gone, and so is the viewer's own serialized Player element that pruneRosterToViewer kept. Measured: no client reads either (useWorldPlay takes state and nothing else; its 'mine' comes from the seat the platform puts on the frame that seats you), while both made every body in a fan-out distinct -- a 500-seat announcement in a public plaza of 200 stalls was 500 encodings and 18.5 MB, 27 ms of JSON.stringify plus 55 ms of parse, for 500 copies of one answer. With them gone the same plaza is ONE body. WorldEngine.viewsFor now answers {bodies, seats}: each distinct view once, plus which one each seat holds, so a host encodes once per body instead of once per watcher; runner.viewsFor answers {bodies, of, refused} in place of a per-player map. Sharing is decided structurally by Game.projectsAlikeForEverySeat (no element declares visibility, no class withholds attributes, no playerView, no tutorial progress, no addressed animation event) and by the seat's declared partitions, never by comparing encoded bodies -- comparing them costs the encoding this removes. A world that hides anything pays exactly what it paid before: a room scoped with addVisibleTo is per-seat output even when every seat is granted, because redactVisibilityForSeat collapses the grant roster to the reader. The conformance case 'viewFor is PER PLAYER' is retired, because two seats of a world with nothing hidden between them SHOULD now receive identical bytes. formatHash is unchanged: stored partition bytes are untouched and a live world crosses this revision with no gate. Platform: read the view as {state, phase} and take the seat from the commands frame.

A read the engine owns runs on the real element behind a read-only projection, and only its answer is projected (ShufflewickPub #409). Binding every method to the proxy charged a trap per step of its own walk, so a finder over 500 roots cost 16x the live tree -- and a world's OFFER is a fan-out of finders, run for every seat a change reaches. Measured on a 500-seat village: an offer fan-out fell from 2277 ms to 125 ms, 4.55 ms a seat to 0.25 ms, which takes the offer half of a per-command fan-out from 11x the view half to below it. ENGINE_READ_DOORS is an allowlist, so a method nobody names is slow and never unsafe; a finder's own predicate is handed projected elements and an element read out of a projection goes back through a door as the element it wraps. Nothing a fingerprint can see changes: no surface, no player-view payload, no stored byte, so all three hashes stand where r65 left them and every live world crosses onto this revision with no gate. Recorded with --adopt so the platform can archive and run the build.

A room scoped with addVisibleTo/addZoneVisibleTo is ONE view for every seat that holds the same grant (ShufflewickPub #411). WIRE CHANGE on the per-seat view only: redactVisibilityForSeat no longer spells the reader's own grant as addPlayers:[yourSeat], it spells it in the MODE and drops the roster entirely -- a granted reader is told 'all', a denied reader the mode that denies everybody (a count-only zone stays count-only, because the serializer shows its count), and a reader named in neither keeps the base mode. That is exactly canPlayerSee's precedence, so every reader is given the answer it was given before, held exhaustively over every mode and roster rather than by sample. The reader learns strictly LESS than the roster told it: nothing in a per-seat view can name another seat any more, and a seat can no longer tell a room it was let into from a room that was public all along. The full roster still round-trips through the checkpoint/restore path (full toJSON), which is what stores a partition. Measured through the engine on a plaza of 200 stalls at 500 seats: the same plaza scoped to every seat was 500 distinct bodies, 70 MB and 324 ms of encode-and-parse, and is now ONE body of 136 KB -- the collapse #408 reached only for a plainly public room, which matters because scoping a room is how most room-shaped worlds are built. Game#projectsAlikeForEverySeat becomes Game#projectsAlikeFor(seats): a grant is about seats, so the audience being asked is part of the question, and visibilityRedactsAlikeFor decides each declared state the way the redaction writes it. Sharing is still decided STRUCTURALLY and is still all-or-nothing for an audience: a room granted to only PART of the audience is one body per seat exactly as before, and a world with genuine per-seat secrets pays what it always paid. formatHash is unchanged: stored partition bytes are untouched and a live world crosses onto this revision with no gate.

The contract's payload fixture now DECLARES who may see what, so a per-seat view's redaction is fingerprinted (ShufflewickPub #414). No engine behaviour changes: this is a fixture and a guard. Until now the fixture's world declared no element or zone visibility anywhere, so redactVisibilityForSeat never ran over anything in it and no visibility/zoneVisibility field reached a fingerprinted view -- r67 rewrote exactly those bytes and payloadHash did not move, and the platform heard about the revision only because an unrelated rename moved the surface. A redaction change on its own would have shipped silently to the vendored clone, which is the one thing this file exists to prevent, and it is the same class of gap as boardsmith/world shipping before it was in PLATFORM_ENTRYPOINTS. The commons now holds two rooms: a wellhouse whose contents are hidden and granted to the first looker, and a noticeboard whose contents are hidden from the second, so ONE fan-out carries a granted reader, an ungranted one and a denied one. assertCoversWorldRedaction fails the fixture if that stops being true -- it asserts that the redaction is load-bearing (one looker holds a room's contents and another does not) and that no body names a seat, because a grant is deliberately spelled so that a granted reader cannot tell a room it was let into from a room that was public all along, and no guard can read the grant back out of the bytes. Also records, where the redaction happens, that a redacted tree restored into a live game (the MCTS search sandbox does this) now reads a granted room as plainly public: neither that nor the old hidden-with-a-grant-to-me was ever true about the other seats, and the checkpoint path that must be exact reads the full toJSON. payloadHash moves and nothing else does: surfaceHash is unchanged because no export moved, and formatHash is unchanged because stored partition bytes are untouched, so a live world crosses onto this revision with no gate.

A room granted to only PART of an audience is one view body per GROUP rather than one per seat (ShufflewickPub #413). Game#projectsAlikeFor(seats) becomes Game#projectionSignaturesFor(seats): one string per seat, in the order asked, where equal strings mean byte-identical projections, and null for the whole audience means the tree consults something about a seat that cannot be summarised so no two seats may be assumed alike. #408 and #411 answered ONE BOOLEAN for a whole audience, so an audience that did not agree about a room fell all the way back to a body per seat -- measured on a plaza of 200 stalls at 500 seats with the plaza granted to half of them, that was TWO distinct answers sent as 500 encodings, 53 MB and 274 ms of encode-and-parse, and is now two bodies of 125 KB. THE SIGNATURE IS THE REDACTION'S OWN OUTPUT, not a hash of a projected body: for each state the tree declares, in one fixed walk order, the MODE redactVisibilityForSeat writes for that seat. That mode is the entirety of what the redaction writes (the roster is dropped and the seat is never named, #411) and it also decides what canPlayerSee answered, since 'all' is written exactly where the answer was yes -- so two seats spelled alike everywhere hold the same bytes, held exhaustively over every mode x every roster x every seat x every owner rather than by sample. An element declaring nothing inherits the nearest declaring ancestor's state, which is already in the signature, so the walk stays local. WHAT REFUSES, and it is refusal rather than approximation: an 'owner' element or zone for every seat it does not grant OUTRIGHT (ownership is a fact about the element, not about the state, and an owner-only zone that denies everybody still shows its children to its owner under their real ids while giving everybody else synthetic ones -- #411's predicate grouped those, which this closes), a class with static visibleAttributes, static playerView, any tutorial progress, and any addressed animation event. WorldEngine.viewsFor is unchanged in shape: it still answers {bodies, seats}, with more sharing behind it. formatHash is unchanged: stored partition bytes are untouched and a live world crosses onto this revision with no gate.

A world-owned phase can declare which SEAT it is about, and read that chair's activity watermark as a bounded point read (ShufflewickPub #423). worldClockAction gains .about(), one chair per round of the same ordered declaration walk .needs() already uses, and ctx.world.activityOf(seat) answers { seat, at, since, inactiveSince, tenancy } for a chair the walk named and refuses undeclared-activity for any other. A seated action carrying an activity round is refused when the world is built, so a player has no road to another seat's watermark. commandPartitions becomes commandNeeds and answers two lists -- partitions, and at most one chair per round -- taking what the host has already answered so the walk terminates in order; WorldCommandStamp and WorldEventStamp carry declaredActivity, and walkDeclaration drives both legs and returns what apply takes. A chair's SINCE is now the later of the world's recording epoch and the instant its holder took it, so a newcomer in an old world is not instantly reapable, and tenancy tells an empty or erased chair from a silent empire (#399, #410).

A text selection can ask for a multiline field: enterText({ multiline: true }) sets an optional multiline flag on a text pick's metadata, and the shared ActionPanel draws a labelled resizable textarea with a character count and an explicit submit button (so Enter inserts a newline) instead of a single-line input. It is presentation only -- the value, minLength/maxLength/pattern and validate are unchanged, and the flag is absent from every pick that does not ask for it -- so a host needs no change to carry it, but a host that draws its own controls from pick metadata should honour it for prose fields. The panel also now reports a text value the length or pattern rules refuse (using the engine's own wording) rather than silently doing nothing, and its length hint states 'up to N characters' where it previously rendered '(?-N chars)'.

The Action Panel gains a game-authored hierarchy for its start buttons: an action declares .group('More', 'Empire settings') and .order(n), and a group takes one button at its level and opens onto its members. Both fields ride on ActionMetadata and on a world's offer, so a re-vendor picks them up on the world path with nothing to change host-side; a bundle that declares no grouping sends none and renders the flat panel it always did. Opening a group is UI navigation only and never a command, so no new engine verb, no new frame and no new host obligation. formatHash is unmoved: no stored partition bytes change.

CLI-side only, and the reason it needs a number is that no fingerprint can see it. `boardsmith pack` and `boardsmith build` now honour an absolute `--out-dir` instead of appending it to the invocation directory: pack wrote its tarball inside the repository and left an untracked directory there, and build was worse, splitting one bundle across two directories so the rules and UI bundles landed at the absolute path while manifest.json and the public/ copy landed inside the project, leaving a bundle that cannot be validated or published. A pack that fails now also leaves nothing behind, neither a stray tarball in the source tree nor an output directory it only created to try. The engine did not change: surfaceHash, payloadHash and formatHash are all carried forward unmoved, and this revision exists solely so the platform can archive a build whose tarball bytes differ from r72's. NOTHING HERE IS URGENT FOR THE PLATFORM. The hosted runtime never runs pack or build, and the vendoring chain packs with --target, which was already correct, so r72 remains a correct engine to run. This is a fix for game authors driving the CLI locally, so re-vendor at your convenience.

r74 is CLI-side only, and the reason it needs a number is the same as r73's: no fingerprint can see it, but the packed tarball's bytes differ from r73's for the same engine. surfaceHash 1feb60c2051e0c9b, payloadHash eaab9ade0d133677 and formatHash 0058593e7cc80205 are all carried forward unmoved. Two fixes to `boardsmith init` (#240). First, <name> is now validated as a NAME rather than joined onto the invocation directory: it is simultaneously the project directory, the package name in package.json, the game's identifier in boardsmith.json and the prefix of every generated class, so it must be kebab-case, and a path-shaped or npm-scoped name is refused up front with the kebab-case form of what was typed offered for the user to copy. `init /tmp/x/mygame` used to create <cwd>/tmp/x/mygame, or write a path into package.json as the package name. `chunk-check <slug>` had the same identity-as-location conflation and refuses a path-shaped slug too. Second, twelve sites across seven commands handed a raw Error object to console.error, printing stack frames and internal paths that CLAUDE.md forbids; a terminal failure now throws for cli.ts's top-level handler to render as one clean line, and the four failures a running dev server recovers from log the message instead. NOTHING HERE IS URGENT FOR THE PLATFORM. The hosted runtime never runs init, build or pack, and no engine behaviour, protocol or payload shape changed, so r72 and r73 both remain correct engines to run. This is a fix for game authors and bs- build sessions driving the CLI locally, so re-vendor at your convenience.

r75 is CLI-side only, and it needs a number for the same reason r73 and r74 did: no fingerprint can see it, but the packed tarball's bytes differ from r74's for the same engine. surfaceHash 1feb60c2051e0c9b, payloadHash eaab9ade0d133677 and formatHash 0058593e7cc80205 are all carried forward unmoved. Two fixes. First, every developer tool boardsmith spawns and reads back (#241): runToolCapturingStdout decoded each arriving chunk of the child's stdout on its own, so a multi-byte UTF-8 character split across a chunk boundary became U+FFFD and the captured report was not what the tool printed. stdout is now buffered whole and decoded once. That silently changed an accepted clone group's key in boardsmith audit --dupes-baseline, which hashes the duplicated source text fallow reports, and it was blamed twice on fallow re-cutting group boundaries instead. Second, boardsmith init no longer leaves a half-scaffolded project behind (#242): a failure after the directory was created left a project whose rulebook/INDEX.md provenance describes an archive that does not exist, and that directory is the very shape init refuses to overwrite, so the retry the user reaches for failed too. It now removes only the tree it had to create, keeps a pre-existing directory because that one is the user's, and prints Created <name> successfully! after the last step that can fail rather than before it. NOTHING HERE IS URGENT FOR THE PLATFORM. The hosted runtime never runs init and never spawns fallow or jscpd, and no engine behaviour, protocol or payload shape changed, so r72, r73 and r74 all remain correct engines to run. This is a fix for game authors and bs- build sessions driving the CLI locally, so re-vendor at your convenience.

r76 is CLI-side only and changes no behaviour at all, but it needs a number for the same reason r73, r74 and r75 did: no fingerprint can see it, and the packed tarball's bytes still differ from r75's for the same engine, because src/ is packed. surfaceHash 1feb60c2051e0c9b, payloadHash eaab9ade0d133677 and formatHash 0058593e7cc80205 are all carried forward unmoved. Two source files, src/cli/lib/dupes-baseline.ts and src/cli/lib/choice-cardinality.ts, each held a literal U+0000 byte as a key separator (#243). NUL is the right separator, since no source text can hold one and so no fragment can forge the delimiter; only its spelling was wrong, and one literal NUL is enough for git to classify a file as binary and leave every change to it undiffable in git diff, git log -p, git show and any review UI. Written as the escape it builds the identical string, which was measured directly against the pre-change module: the same key, and .fallow-dupes-accepted.json is not in the diff at all, with 1085 accepted groups before and after, nothing re-keyed and nothing forgiven. A gate now scans every tracked text file for control bytes other than tab, line feed and carriage return, because this mistake got in twice. THE PLATFORM DOES NOT NEED THIS. shufflewick.pub never spawns fallow or jscpd, never reaches either module, and no engine behaviour, protocol or payload shape changed, so r72 through r75 all remain correct engines to run. Re-vendor whenever it is convenient, or not at all.

World views are published before action-offer enumeration: world_state drops actions and carries a revision, and offers arrive on a new world_offers frame stamped with the state they were enumerated over (#244).

A cross-root migration may be run in BOUNDED memory, a page at a time (ShufflewickPub #449). world.migration gains survey: { initial(), root(digest, element, name), maxBytes } -- a fold of every existing root into ONE bounded, JSON-serializable digest, run BEFORE anything is written, with the element handed over read-only through readonly.ts's projection so a write is the declaration-write refusal rather than a silent no-op. partition() and create() are then handed the COMPLETED digest on their context, so every write is a pure function of (that root, that digest) and iteration order cannot matter. survey and finalize are mutually exclusive, refused at declaration. runner.migrationNeedsEveryRoot() is REPLACED by runner.migrationShape(), which tells all three shapes apart: independent (page in one pass), survey (page in TWO passes, carrying the digest between calls as bytes) and whole-world (finalize, every root in one call). migrateAll's context gains pass, digest and maxDigestBytes; WorldMigrated gains digest, and a survey pass answers NO partition bytes and NO created roots. A digest past survey.maxBytes or past the host's own lower ceiling is refused naming the size, the bound and whose it was. WorldEngine gains surveyPartition(). The declaration-write refusal message now names every read-only surface rather than only a declaration. New worldMigration() helper infers the digest type into every hook.

Two additions. (1) A migration may split one source root into a header plus the durable roots it fans out into: WorldMigration.derive(element, ctx) runs per source root on the transform page that holds it, BEFORE partition and on the root exactly as stored, and returns new durable roots that merge into WorldMigrated.created -- so every transform page may now answer created, not only the final creation page. ctx.existing names every root the world holds plus every root already derived on that page, so a re-sent page is refused and forward-only resume stays safe. An unanswered top-level allocation in any migration hook (partition, derive, create, finalize) is now refused naming the element and the hook, rather than silently dropped (#246). (2) A chooseFrom can ask for an ORDERED, REPEATABLE list of choices: orderedList: { min, max } bounds ENTRIES rather than distinct identities, so one identity may appear more than once and the handler receives the sequence as submitted, each occurrence validated against the same authoritative choices. multiSelect is untouched and still refuses a repeated choice. A pick carries orderedList instead of multiSelect on the wire, and the Action Panel draws it as Add buttons over a numbered, removable list; a board click appends through the same shared draft (#249) (3) A world action may QUOTE the draft in front of a player before it commits (#248). New .quote(fn) on worldAction: one function of the args the player has drafted so far -- a number typed into the panel's editor and not yet submitted included, an omitted optional selection still absent -- answered as the lines to show them, run under the same read-only facilities and projection an offer's callbacks run under, so a quote that writes is refused. WorldEngine gains quotePartitions() and resolveQuote() (the whole declaration walk, including the execute round, hydrated with the draft bound); the runner gains declareQuote()/resolveQuote(); the wire gains world_quote / world_quote_result, which the platform host must relay for a world's panel to show a price. An offer carries quote: true, and both the shared action panel and a custom UI then CONFIRM rather than auto-committing on the last pick, refusing to submit a draft whose price is not on screen. ActionMetadata gains quote; useActionController gains actionQuote/quotePending/quoteError/awaitingConfirmation/confirmDisabledReason/confirm() as shared state, and the panel's optional number/text editor finally draws the skip control its own '(optional)' label promised.

A new platform-owned refusal, world-state-unreadable (#257). A host that versions a piece of a world's durable state had no code for finding one written in a shape this worker does not read, so the condition arrived as a bare Error and ownerOf called it the GAME's - which dead-lettered an event the bundle's code had never been asked to run, and downstream (ShufflewickPub #464) left a player told a definitively failed request 'may still have gone through'. PLATFORM-owned, so a host's ladder parks it: the same bytes meet the same reader on every wake, so retrying is the one response that cannot work and parking after two is what stops a world spending a wake an hour on it. Deliberately NOT infrastructure, which is forgiven on a timer because somebody else's service coming back is the repair, and not game-owned, which world-migration-unavailable already is for the version gap that IS the bundle's. The park/drain question is settled in the table rather than per host: such a world is still drained and still parked, because the condition is only discoverable by reading and every event that does not read the key is the rest of the world's ordinary business. New worldStateUnreadable({ key, storedVersion, readableVersion }) raises it and takes those three things and nothing else, so what the state held - player data, on its way into a log - cannot be interpolated into the sentence; storedVersion null means state that predates versioning. surfaceHash only: no stored byte and no player-view payload changes.
enterNumber can open a field on a starting value and label each value in its range (#258): number picks now carry optional initial and valueLabels on the wire.

ActionBuilder gains .destructive() (issue 268): an action can mark itself as one that permanently ends something, and the flag rides the actionMetadata channel as ActionMetadata.destructive and on a world's offer frame. The Action Panel paints such a verb from the new dedicated --bsg-destructive-surface / --bsg-destructive-ink token pair and adds an inset ring, a marker glyph and a screen-reader label, so the warning is not carried by colour alone; a custom board reads the same flag off the same metadata. Presentation only: availability, validation and execution are unchanged.

A world action's DECLARATION can now read the scheduled occurrence it is running (#271): WorldDeclarationFacilities carries timing alongside now, so a clock handler's needs() and about() rounds read world.timing and a rate-producing catch-up names one partition per folded occurrence instead of guessing a fixed ceiling and silently losing the work past it. commandNeeds and WorldRunnerHandle.declare take a WorldDispatchWhen -- { kind: 'arrival', now } for a seat's command, { kind: 'scheduled', timing } for the clock -- so the walk and the apply that follows it cannot disagree about the instant or the fold; a clock dispatch declared as an arrival is refused with the new platform-owned untimed-clock-declaration.

A migration may rebuild an EXISTING root from another root's exact ORIGINAL records, a page at a time (issue 275). #449's survey is a FOLD, so an exact join -- "this root's new value is those particular records, held by those other roots" -- could only be expressed by putting the corpus in the digest, which a host refuses: the reported reproduction measured a complete join at 524,401 bytes against the platform's 262,144-byte ceiling, and derive may not replace an existing root, finalize may not page, and a cold transform page could name no other root at all. world.migration gains join: { sources(name, digest), maxSources }: each root DECLARES which original roots its transform reads, from its name and the completed digest alone -- never from its own contents, because a host asks while deciding what to load -- and ctx.source(name) on the partition and derive contexts then answers that root AS IT WAS STORED WHEN THE MIGRATION BEGAN, read-only, through readonly.ts's projection. New runner.migrationSources(page, { digest, maxSources }) answers the exact union a transform page must carry, is pure and repeatable so a cold resume asks for the same page, and migrateAll's context gains sources (those originals, by name) and maxSources (the host's own lower ceiling). A transform page of a joining migration is refused without them, refused when what it carries is not what the page declared in either direction, and a hook reading an original it did not declare is refused by name. join and finalize are mutually exclusive, refused at declaration; a root may not name itself; a survey pass sent originals is refused. migrationShape() gains an optional joins: { maxSources } on the two pageable kinds, so a host learns before it starts that it must serve originals stably across pages. WorldEngine gains migrateSources(supplied, run), which hydrates the originals into a SECOND, empty game -- an original's element ids are the ids the live root already holds, and one identity may not be in a tree twice -- scoped to the call so nothing can keep them. createWorld supplies that second game from the bundle's own game class. THE HOST CONTRACT IS NEW WORK: a platform must serve a joining migration's originals from the world as it stood when the migration began, however many roots it has already rewritten, and may not run such a migration until it can. No stored byte and no player-view payload changes; payloadHash moves only because WORLD_DURABILITY_FIXTURE gains the join page's context, which is a type surfaceHash cannot see.

Elements and the game root can declare static seatAttributes (#269): a per-seat DERIVED attribute, a name-to-function map evaluated at projection time with the live element and the receiving seat (null for a spectator), whose value is merged into that seat's node after the visibleAttributes whitelist and stored nowhere. visibleAttributes is a whitelist over STORED attributes, so a value gated on a fact that can change had to be stored already-gated and re-derived by every write path that could change the gate -- a world character's coordinate readout gated on carrying a GPS unit kept its stale figure when another seat's command emptied the pack, and was served until that seat happened to issue a command that rewrote it. A derivation is asked at serialization instead, so there is nothing to keep in step: returning undefined leaves the attribute out of that seat's view, toJSON() and stored world partitions never carry one, and a restore of a per-seat view does not turn one back into a stored field. It runs on the single per-seat path (toJSONForPlayer, the batched toJSONForPlayers under it, snapshots taken forSeat, a bot's redacted clone and a world's viewFor), never for an element the seat cannot see, and projectionSignaturesFor now refuses an audience whose tree declares one, the same way it refuses visibleAttributes and playerView. Refused loudly at projection: a derived name the element also stores or the engine owns, a derivation that throws (the error names class, attribute and seat), and a value JSON cannot carry (the error names the path inside it).

An action is offered on its first unsatisfied step: a later chooseFrom returning [] before its input exists no longer removes the verb from a seat's offer (table and world), and the pruning that remains warns with the action and question named (#270)

The world clock can finalize a vacancy for a chair the host itself vouched for (ShufflewickPub #475): world.vacateByClock names one seatless verb -- checked at createWorld to exist, to be built with worldClockAction() and to declare a chair with .about() -- and only that verb may call the new ctx.world.vacate(seat) on WorldClockFacilities, which admits exactly the chairs activityOf admits (one the declaration asked about and the host answered a point read for), resolves the roster key from the engine's own roster rather than letting a bundle name a player, and reports it to the host as WorldCommandResult.vacated = { seat, player } on the same result the dirty set rides, so the chair is released on the checkpoint that proves the ground came back; a host stamp of tenancy 'empty' makes the call a no-op so a completion retried after a cold wake releases exactly once, a second different chair in one dispatch is refused with vacancy-already-claimed, any other verb with not-the-vacancy-verb, and a chair this world seats nobody in with vacancy-unheld; createWorld now also reports vacateByClock beside vacate, and the seated world.vacate road is unchanged.

A world bundle can declare its referral verbs (ShufflewickPub #473): world.referral = { founding, onGrant } is typed by WorldDefinition and exported as WorldReferralDeclaration from boardsmith/world, and readWorldDefinition hands the block back exactly as the bundle wrote it -- the engine reads nothing from it and checks neither name, because whether a founding earns a reward and which verbs a host may issue is host policy, as it is for presence; the host is the one that refuses a non-seated founding or a non-seatless onGrant.

A joining migration's cost is declared in BYTES and the host's count ceiling is gone (ShufflewickPub #487). world.migration.join gains a required maxSourceBytes: the most the originals ONE root names may weigh together. migrationShape().joins carries it beside maxSources, so a host admits or refuses a joining version against the figure that actually binds one call, before any marker exists, and holds the migration to it while it pages. The host-stated COUNT ceiling is removed: WorldMigrateContext.maxSources and WorldMigrationSourcesContext.maxSources are gone, migrationSources(page, { digest }) takes no ceiling, and declaredSources enforces the author's join.maxSources alone. #476's host derived its count by dividing the page budget by the largest a root may be, which prices every original as a maximal root -- ShufflewickPub #487 measured a thirty-six-source join at 625,119 bytes refused against a ceiling of three on a page carrying 1,835,008. A root's stored size is a fact only a host has, so the host measures the bytes and the library declares them; no second measurement is made here. No stored byte and no player-view payload changes; payloadHash moves because WorldMigrateContext lost a field.

A chronological world's checkpoint drain re-reads the committed queue before every entry instead of dispatching a once-selected snapshot (#280), so an entry cancelled or displaced by an earlier entry in the same drain no longer fires and a later event can no longer commit ahead of an earlier one the preceding checkpoint scheduled. Also carries the projection trap-count test (#281) and GameShell's platform-mode game_ready hello (ShufflewickPub #486). No exported surface, player-view payload or stored byte moves, which is why the platform cannot reach this build without a number of its own.

A world's action panel says when its verbs are still arriving (#282). While useWorldHost.offersPending is true, ActionPanel renders "Working out what you can do here..." on data-testid="bs-actions-pending" with role="status" in place of the button list; PlayShell forwards the new optional actionsPending prop and WorldShell binds it to the same ref a custom board reads. A table never sets it, so GameShell is unchanged and an empty button list on a table still means what it always meant. The two-frame publication contract (#244) puts a world's offers seconds behind the projection they are enumerated over -- measured at 3.1s, 7.4s and up to 13s cold -- and a world commits several times over an attach, so the panel legitimately fills in stages; what was wrong was that it rendered markup identical to "this seat may do nothing" in between. No exported surface, player-view payload or stored byte moves, which is why the platform cannot reach this build without a number of its own.

A world's rules and its runner must share one engine (#283): createWorld refuses a gameClass that does not extend this engine's Game with the new platform-owned WorldRefusal code "engine-mismatch", which is the one exported-surface change here. Also carries the engine fix that a class finder (first/all/firstN/last/lastN with a class and a predicate) runs its predicates only on elements of that class instead of every element walked, and boardsmith dev's world host now being bundled with the rules so it runs on their engine. On a 1,600-sector world that took boardsmith dev from 4-132 s per command to under 250 ms. No player-view payload or stored byte moves.

A world's declarations, views and offers read an element's class as that class (#285). The read-only projection used to wrap every function it handed back, classes included, so element.constructor inside a declaration was an anonymous wrapper with no name or static members, and game.first(element.constructor) treated it as a predicate and threw where the same line in execute found the element. Classes now pass through the projection unchanged; methods are still wrapped and a mutating one is still refused. No exported surface, player-view payload or stored byte moves; the platform must run this build for its world runner to get the fix.

A flow step can declare how long it stays open (#300). actionStep and simultaneousActionStep accept timeLimitMs (a number, or a function resolved once at step entry); the resolved duration is kept in the step's position.frameData, rides FlowState.timeLimitMs, and SnapshotSessionHost broadcast meta carries turnBoundary.timeLimitMs (absent for an untimed step; the boundary key is unchanged). payloadHash moved only because the contract fixture now declares a window. boardsmith build stamps a NEW capability, capabilities.timedSteps, from the compiled flow, and build and validate refuse a timed game without idleAction. The platform must add timedSteps to GameCapabilities/CAPABILITY_KEYS when it vendors this revision, or validateCapabilities refuses every bundle built on it (ShufflewickPub #505). Not breaking: no existing field moved.

A step's timeLimitMs has a floor of ten seconds (#307). boardsmith exports MIN_STEP_TIME_LIMIT_MS (10000); a fixed limit under it is refused when the flow is built (so build and validate refuse it) and a function's answer under it is refused when the step is entered, naming the step. The platform runs its own copy of the engine, so no table can arm a shorter window and the platform can hold its round-expiry budget against this constant (ShufflewickPub #505). Not breaking: no existing field moved.

The contract fixture now produces two world facts it had missed, found when #312 type-checked it for the first time: world_command carries order (a paid order's id and instant, #195), and the watching seat's activity watermark is rendered by a pick prompt (an action prompt takes only a string, so the old one was a function JSON dropped and the watermark moved no hash). payloadHash moved only because the fixture now produces these bytes; no engine behavior changed. Not breaking.

SnapshotSessionHost persists and restores each seat's in-progress multi-step selection (#320). New exported type SnapshotHostState { snapshot, flowState, pendingStates } is what the persist adapter now receives, what the new durableState() method returns, and what restoreFrom() now REQUIRES (pendingStates is no longer optional to omit; pass {} when no seat is mid-action). restoreFrom refuses pending states keyed by anything but a seat of this table. A failed action that cleared a seat's pending selection now persists that change. Platforms must store pendingStates with the snapshot and pass them back on restore, or a player who pauses mid-action loses their picks.

The flow state no longer reports a leftover single-seat prompt during a simultaneous step (#321): FlowState.currentPlayer and availableActions are published only while an action step is awaiting input, so they are absent in a simultaneous step and once the game is complete. Before this, a simultaneous step entered after an action step kept that step's seat and actions, so GameShell showed a seat that had already acted in the step (or had no entry) the previous step's actions, and the random simulator got stuck on every cribbage game. The contract fixture now also hashes the whole-game flow state the executor returns, which is what made this visible. Not breaking: re-vendor to pick up the fix.
getFlowDebugInfo names the step the engine is actually at; FlowEngine's private path-navigation helpers moved to one shared rule (#324)
Removed validateFlowPosition and formatFlowRecovery from 'boardsmith': nothing called them, and no dev host recovers a truncated flow position that way (#342)

A repeating selection (chooseFrom/chooseElement with repeat or repeatUntil) now means one thing on every path that submits a move (#325): a whole 'action' op, a bot's move (botTurn), the random simulator and enumerateLegalMoves run each pick through onEach exactly as step-by-step picks do, and execute receives the picks as an array ending at the terminator (a repeating chooseElement's picks arrive as elements). A whole submission must send that array; a scalar or an unfinished repeat is refused by name, and a refusal after onEach ran is rolled back (ActionResult.threw and FlowState.actionThrew are renamed partiallyApplied and actionPartiallyApplied). ActionExecutor gains repeatingPickCandidates and pendingActionRefusal. The argument is now typed as an array (#347). Not breaking for built bundles: re-vendor so bots on the platform play repeats like humans.

boardsmith/world exports the presence departure grace: WORLD_PRESENCE_DEFAULT_GRACE_MS (60s), WORLD_PRESENCE_MIN_GRACE_MS (1s), WORLD_PRESENCE_MAX_GRACE_MS (24h) and presenceDepartGraceMs(), so the platform and boardsmith dev share one default and range (#338).

Two engine changes (#352, #334). A repeating selection's own validate now runs once per pick on every path that submits a move: it receives the pick (an element for chooseElement) with the picks made before it in args, a refused pick runs no onEach, a whole submission containing one is refused as 'Pick N of "name": <message>', and bots, the simulator and enumerateLegalMoves never offer it; a repeating chooseElement's callbacks now see earlier picks as elements. And chooseFrom, chooseElement and chooseElements (and the world facade's versions) take prepare(ctx), run once per evaluation of the choices, whose result is disabled's third argument, disabled(choice, ctx, prepared); a prepare without a disabled rule is refused at declaration. Re-vendor before running a game that uses prepare: an older engine ignores it and hands disabled undefined.

Mapping a submitted value onto a choice (ActionExecutor.resolveArgs, resolveSelectionValue) no longer evaluates the selection's disabled rule or prepare for every candidate (#364): it reads the candidates through the new candidatesOf, so a whole move judges a chooseFrom's choices three times instead of five. No change to what is accepted or refused.

boardsmith and boardsmith/session no longer export the dev state-transfer API (captureDevState, restoreDevState, validateDevSnapshot, formatValidationErrors, getSnapshotElementCount, createDevCheckpoint, restoreFromDevCheckpoint, DevCheckpointManager); nothing called it after boardsmith dev began reloading table rules through a snapshot restore or replay (#343, #362).

PlayerGameState gains gameInstanceId (and GameStateSnapshot carries it): a random id minted when a game starts, kept across undo and every stateless op, and new on every start including a start from a --seed position. GameShell tears down an open pick when it or restoreEpoch changes, so a new game at the same step no longer offers the previous game's element ids (#356).
